source.title: MoME: Mixture-of-Memory Embeddings for Context-Aware Sparse Lookup
source.authors: Mu-Chen Li; Leonid Sigal; Ren-Jie Liao

page_placements.theme: Memory, state and representation capacity provide additional scaling axes

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some table and figure content is flattened, but the memory-scaling table is legible.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the original scaling-law works and reports a memory-capacity sweep, but it does not test or rely on the claim’s power laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or fit dependence.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own memory-parameter scaling sweep, but it does not fit or test a power law in language-model parameter count, training tokens, or training compute. The sweep is recorded under fits_no_version rather than linked to a claim version. Other pretraining and downstream benchmark results are not rows because they do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a memory-embedding module (MoME) and compares it with other memory baselines. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as motivation. Its 'memory-size scaling' sweep varies auxiliary memory-table parameters at a fixed 135M backbone and fixed 3e18 FLOPs. It fits no power law, tests no extrapolation and does not vary total parameters, tokens or compute in the sense the versions name. The dense-scaling controls (Table 19) and the 100B-token runs are method comparisons, not tests of scaling laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MoME beats memory baselines and shows a 'more favorable memory-size scaling trend' than Bigram within the tested sub-billion regime. They make no claim about standard LM scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The reported sweep scales conditional-memory capacity at fixed nanochat d12 backbone and training compute; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurement or fit power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Memory method (MoME versus Bigram) and memory capacity vary across the sweep; MoME has lower validation BPB than matched-memory Bigram at each reported size.

fits_no_version.finding: Setup: nanochat d12 backbone at 3e18 FLOPs, with auxiliary memory scaled from 75.5M to 604M parameters. Validation bpb falls monotonically for both methods: Bigram from 0.8672 to 0.8571, MoME from 0.8669 to 0.8533. MoME is lower than Bigram at every size, and the gains diminish. No power law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding sparse token-indexed memory parameters at a fixed backbone and fixed compute lowers validation loss, with diminishing returns; how much depends on the memory method.

record.problems: The memory-size sweep is limited to a single nanochat-style backbone and fixed training compute; it tests memory capacity rather than standard model-size, token-count, or compute scaling laws. The paper reports three-seed standard deviations for this sweep but does not fit power-law curves or assess extrapolation.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against model parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to large ones.
No sweep of depth or width at fixed parameter count. Table 19 dense width controls change parameter count and are method baselines.
Text pretraining only; no other modalities or training regimes.
CORE is reported alongside bpb, but there is no analysis of downstream predictability from scale or loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation and tranche (cites_only, T6) are confirmed. The word 'scaling' in this paper refers to memory-table capacity, not the Kaplan or Chinchilla axes. The rows are a method comparison of the authors' own module against baselines and arguably should not be claim rows at all. They are kept only as support for the fits_no_version entry.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling in model parameters, training tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger-run losses from fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of published scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

relation.reason: The introduction cites Hoffmann and Kaplan to motivate dense scaling. The study reports memory-module experiments without testing or applying their scaling laws.

tranche.reason: The auxiliary-memory sweep compares method performance at fixed backbone and training compute. It does not test power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or another listed version; it does not use a fitted scaling law as a tool.

source_check.notes: All reported values, uncertainties, baselines and conditions match Table 17. The rows are method-performance comparisons with no claim-version link; the authors' conclusion is accurately summarized.
